paragraphs: Now that I have finished all my clerkships at the Medical University of Gdansk and returned to Japan, I keenly feel how precious those exciting days were, a series of encounters with "others who break you." Before studying abroad, I had almost no knowledge of Poland, let alone Gdansk. The only image I had of Poland was as the country visited by the protagonist 財前五郎 in the 2003 TV drama "The Great White Tower" to attend an international surgical conference. Gdansk is the largest port city in Poland, located in northern Poland, and is historically known as the place where the Second World War broke out. The Medical University of Gdansk, in Gdansk, is a university founded in 1945 that originates from a medical facility centered on surgeons established around 1454.

As preparation before studying abroad, I attended pre-departure training given by doctors who had studied abroad in the past, and studied medical English by watching videos explaining medicine in English. Also, because I was anxious about English listening, I tried to be exposed to the sounds of English daily by repeatedly watching Western films and listening to podcasts. As for procedures, thinking that I must not break the image that "Japanese are dexterous" if I had a chance to show it locally, I also practised things like laparoscopic ligation. Even so, I always carried in my heart the conflict of "Is it really all right that it is me who goes to Gdansk?", and spent days with more anxiety than expectation.

When I arrived in Gdansk, local students helped carry my luggage to the dormitory. In the evening they showed me around the hospital grounds and took me to a famous cafe in the old town. At this point my English was still poor, so I remember that every day I tried to imitate and adopt the English expressions of the local students. The Medical University of Gdansk has a Polish Division made up of Polish students and an English Division made up of international students, and I did my clerkships mixed in with the English Division. In the English Division, all lectures are given in English. The students' countries of origin were varied, such as Norway, Switzerland, India, Spain and Kazakhstan, and even while in Poland I could place myself in an internationally colorful environment. On this study abroad I did clerkships for one to two weeks each in neurosurgery, surgery, transplant surgery, urology, gastroenterology, cardiology, anesthesiology and pediatric surgery. Being able to do clerkships in many departments is, I think, one of the attractions of the Medical University of Gdansk. The content of the clerkships was mainly lectures, ward clerkships, outpatient observation and surgical observation, like the clinical clerkships at Nagoya University. What left a particular impression was anesthesiology. I had originally not planned to do a clerkship in anesthesiology, but when I observed a certain operation, I was impressed to see the anesthesiologist working while communicating well with the surgeons and nurses, so I negotiated directly with the anesthesiologist and was allowed to do a clerkship. In the operating room I was allowed to experience procedures such as intubation and was taught about maintaining anesthesia enthusiastically and logically. Hearing the doctor say "As an anesthesiologist, I work respecting all the staff," I felt anew the high humanity of the local anesthesiologists. Also, on the last day of each block there were written examinations and oral examinations. I managed to prepare by speaking to students in the same group and getting information about the exams. The cardiology exam in particular was one that the local students all said was difficult, and it required interpreting ECGs. In the cardiology ward clerkship, the doctor gave us many ECGs and we discussed the findings within the group. Breaking out in a cold sweat, giving my ECG findings in unfamiliar English is also a good memory now. On the last day I could answer almost all of the doctor's questions, and I felt I had grown. What was impressive when watching the local students was their high level of independence. The local students freely speak up and ask questions even in the middle of lectures. The length of the breaks between lectures can also be decided freely by the students negotiating with the teacher. They have kept the ability to speak freely that I lost as I grew older. I remember being strongly shocked by seeing that fact. I too hesitated at first, but gradually I began to regain that ability, became able to state my opinions actively, and felt my own regeneration.

Locally, I was greatly helped by Professor Woźniak, who has accepted exchange students from Nagoya University for many years. Professor Woźniak gave me a bag packed with daily necessities, such as frying pans and tableware, left by those who had studied at the Medical University of Gdansk in the past, which was very useful in my daily life. Besides that, he always cared whether I was in any trouble, and on weekends he allowed me to do experiments together with local students, so he helped me both in life and academically. He also held an event called Nagoya Day for local students, and gave me a valuable opportunity to give a presentation about sushi and Japanese tea. The dormitory was a two-person room with a shower and toilet that I was allowed to use alone, so I felt no inconvenience. The dormitory matrons were all truly kind people, and by talking with them at the front desk I received energy every day. Also, prices in Poland are low and students from Nagoya University receive a scholarship of a not small amount, so I think the financial burden is relatively light. To recall my life there, I reread the diary I had been writing at the time. In the early entries there were days when I could not blend into European culture and felt like an alien from another planet, and days when I was shocked to realise that Japan's material abundance had made me nearly lose my own spiritual richness. Through various encounters, the common sense formed by my many years of life in Japan was smashed to pieces, and every day I created a new self by taking in the good parts of European culture. I think the exciting experience of feeling myself changing for sure while struggling with culture shock was possible precisely because I studied abroad. When I looked at the entry I wrote two weeks before returning home, it said, "If I am allowed, I want to stay here longer. And above all I do not want to let the connections I have newly made here break." Before leaving I had only anxiety, and in the early days, to be honest, I wanted to go back to Japan quickly every day. Even I, though, was blessed with wonderful encounters with local people and could experience various new emotions. My life abroad could not be called glittering, but it had a definite feeling of being alive. I am grateful to Dr. 若林, who connected me with the Medical University of Gdansk, Dr. 粕谷 and Dr. 長谷川 of the International Collaboration Office, everyone who supported me greatly in Japan, and all the encounters in Gdansk that confronted one Japanese person head-on and taught me the courage to step out of my comfort zone. May the ties between the Medical University of Gdansk and Nagoya University last for a long time.
